web.title: Improving physical stability of pea protein-based emulsions near the isoelectric point via polysaccharide complexation
web.description:
Many protein-based beverages are formulated under strongly acidic or alkaline conditions, which may cause astringency and off-flavour issues (Carter, Foegeding, & Drake, 2020;Cosson, Souchon, Richard, Descamps, & Saint-Eve, 2020). Therefore formulations at mildly acidic conditions (pH 4.0 to 5.0) are desired in those beverages. This pH range, however, falls in the region of isoelectric point (IEP) for many plant proteins. It is well known that the emulsifying properties of plant proteins are weak at pH values close to their IEP, where a minimal surface charge of the proteins results in extensive droplet flocculation and emulsion destabilization (Chang, Tu, Ghosh, & Nickerson, 2015). In addition, Lan, Chen, and Rao (2018) showed that proteins in PPI aggregated at pH close to its IEP during heat treatment and caused sedimentation in beverages. To overcome this problem, protein-polysaccharide complexation has been proposed to improve the solubility of proteins. For instance, casein aggregation during the storage of acidified milk was prevented with the addition of pectin (Sejersen et al., 2007). More importantly, emulsion stability can be achieved on a broader pH range in the presence of protein-polysaccharide interactions. Gharsallaoui et al. (2010) showed that pectin-coated pea protein isolate (PPI)-stabilized emulsions remained stable against creaming and droplet aggregation between pH 2.4 and pH 6.0 due to strong electrostatic and steric repulsion while only-PPI-stabilized emulsions destabilized near the protein IEP. Furthermore, the denaturation temperature of the PPI-high methoxyl pectin soluble complex was found to be higher than PPI alone (Lan et al., 2018). This shows that complexation may also increase the thermal stability of proteins which is highly desirable in beverage formulations.

In the present work, four different polysaccharides commonly used for manufacturing plant-based beverages (sugar beet pectin, guar gum, gum arabic, gellan gum), with a range of surface charges at different pH values, were chosen to investigate their interactions with pea proteins. Our first aim was to investigate the effect of heat treatment on the complexation of pea protein isolate (PPI) with sugar beet pectin, guar gum, gum arabic, and gellan gum. Sugar beet pectin was chosen, as it is known to have a poorer gelling ability but improved emulsifying properties compared to citrus pectin (Pacheco, Villamiel, Moreno, & Moreno, 2019). Secondly, their emulsification ability was determined by preparing the emulsions with the selected protein-polysaccharide complexes at both basic (pH 8.0) and mildly acidic (pH 4.5) conditions. It was hypothesized that by complexing the proteins with the polysaccharides, it would be possible to stabilize emulsions near the isoelectric point (pI around pH 4.5) of the proteins. As heat treatment is required in beverage applications, the present work also investigated the emulsification behaviour of the pea protein-polysaccharide complexes prepared with heat-treated biopolymers. To our knowledge, no study has investigated both the effect of heat treatment and the emulsification ability of various PPI-polysaccharide complexes at high alkaline pH and the near the pI of the protein.

Complexation behaviour of PPI and pectin The addition of pectin also decreased the EEP of the pectin-PPI complex down to pH 2.3 at the 1:1 mixing ratio from pH 4.7 for PPI alone (Table 1, Fig. 1B). For this study, we used anionic sugar beet pectin with a DE 55%, whose pKa value is around pH 3.5 (Lan et al., 2018). Pectin-PPI complexes (both 1:1 and 1:10 w/w) showed lower OD than PPI (Fig. 1B) and GA-PPI complexes. A previous study showed that the complexation of soy protein isolates with pectin significantly increased protein solubility in the range of pH 4 to 5 (Jaramillo, Roberts, & Coupland, 2011).

complexes The equilibrium interfacial tension was lowered from 22.4 mN/m (for oil-water) to 11.4, 5.7, 9.0, 10.0, and 9.7 with PPI, pectin, GA, pectin-PPI, and GA-PPI at pH 8.0, respectively (Fig. 3). The lowest interfacial tension was observed for pectin, followed by GA, their complexes and PPI. As previously reported, sugar beet pectin is a surface active anionic biopolymer due to the presence of ferulic acid-araban/ galactan-protein complexes that acts as a hydrophobic anchor to the oil droplet (Chen, Fu, & Luo, 2016). Also, it has been proposed that the acetyl and methyl groups on the pectin molecules adsorb onto the oil phase while the charged hydrophilic chain extends towards the aqueous phase (Alba & Kontogiorgos, 2017;Alba, Sagis, & Kontogiorgos, 2016).

Overall, our findings indicate that the proteins, polysaccharides and their mixtures were surface active at both the pH values studied and able to lower oil-water interfacial tension compared to the pure oil-water interface without any biopolymers. 3.4. Emulsification properties of PPI-polysaccharide complexes The emulsion formation and stabilization behaviour of 1:1 pectin-PPI and GA-PPI complexes were tested at pH 4.5 and pH 8.0 and compared against the emulsifying properties of PPI and the polysaccharides alone at the same pH values. No emulsion could be studied with PPI at pH 4.5 due to extensive protein aggregation and emulsion destabilization.

web.title: Fabrication of curcumin-loaded pea protein-pectin ternary complex for the stabilization and delivery of β‑carotene emulsions
web.description:
Coalescence, creaming, and aggregation occurred for emulsions stabilized with proteins at pH value close to the isoelectric point of proteins or high ionic strength condition (Dickinson, 2010). Fabrication of soluble protein-polysaccharide complexes or protein-polysaccharide conjugate may be promising approaches for enhancing the physical stability of emulsions (Evans, Ratcliffe, & Williams, 2013). Fan et al. synthesized covalently linked whey protein-dextran conjugate for BC stabilization and delivery, and they found that whey protein-dextran can significantly enhance the physical stability against environmental conditions including pH close to isoelectric point, high salt concentration, and thermal treatment (Fan, Yi, Zhang, Wen, & Zhao, 2017).

Pectin, acidic polysaccharide, mainly composed of a linear chain of (1→4)-linked α-D-galactopyranosyluronic acid units , is a valuable functional food ingredient extensively utilized as a gelling agent and emulsion stabilizer (Willats, Knox, & Mikkelsen, 2006). The isoelectric point of PPI has been reported to be approximately pH 4.6 (Lan, Chen, & Rao, 2018). High methoxyl pectin (HMP), with a degree of esterification (DE) approximately 60%, was used as an anionic polysaccharide in this study due to its widespread application for the stabilization of acidic milk drinks (Leroux, Langendorff, Schick, Vaishnav, & Mazoyer, 2003;Willats et al., 2006). The pKa of carboxyl moieties in HMP ranges from 2.9 to 3.3 (Lan et al., 2018).

PPI powder (13 mg/mL) was dissolved in ultrapure water and magnetically stirred at least for 1 h at room temperature. The pH of protein solution was adjusted to pH 12 with NaOH (1 M) and kept for half hour. Then, the solution was heated at 88 °C for half hour with a thermostat water bath to lead to the unfolding and refolding of pea protein. After that, the solution was cooled to room temperature immediately and the pH was adjusted back to pH 7. PPI solution was centrifuged at 1600 g/min for 15 min to remove any insoluble ingredient. During pH-shifting process, PPI undergo partial unfolding and then refolding to assume a molten globule conformation that has unique surface properties (Goto, Calciano, & Fink, 1990;Jiang, Chen, & Xiong, 2009). In fact, water solubility of PPI has been remarkably increased after pH-shifting process.

Previous study also indicated that the emulsions stabilized with PPI exhibited better spray dry and storage stability with protective pectin coating (Gharsallaoui, Saurel, Chambin, Cases, Voilley, & Cayot, 2010;Gharsallaoui, Yamauchi, et al., 2010).

web.title: Complexation mechanism of pectins with varying esterification degrees and pea protein isolate: Effects on protein solubility, emulsifying properties, and emulsion stability
web.description:
Abstract The limited solubility and interfacial instability of pea protein isolate (PPI) in neutral and acidic environments considerably restrict its application in structured food products. Therefore, this study aims to enhance the performance of PPI by complexing it with pectin of varying degrees of esterification (DE): high (HDP), medium (MDP), and low (LDP). The interactions between PPI and pectin with different DEs were systematically examined using multiple spectroscopic techniques. Furthermore, microstructure observation, rheological properties, and stability analysis were conducted to evaluate the influence of different pectins on the performance of PPI-based emulsions. The results showed that pectin with different DE could effectively enhance the solubility of PPI and improve the stability of its emulsion. HDP primarily formed complexes with PPI via strong hydrophobic interactions, supplemented by hydrogen bonding. In contrast, LDP enhanced electrostatic interactions with PPI through its higher charge density under suitable conditions. At pH 4.5, HDP increased the solubility of the complex from 7.2% to 42.3%, exhibiting the strongest solubilising effect on PPI. The emulsion stabilised by P1H1 (PPI-HDP complex at a 1:1 mass ratio) exhibited optimal performance within the pH 6.0–7.0 range and maintained high stability over 28 days of storage, with minimal phase separation. In summary, the DE of pectin significantly influences the functional properties of PPI-pectin composite systems by modulating the interaction patterns. This study provides an important theoretical foundation and practical strategies for developing high-quality plant-based food systems.

Despite these advantages, the practical application of PPI in food products such as plant-based beverages, emulsified sauces, and dairy alternatives is often constrained by its low solubility (Li et al., 2022), particularly under neutral and acidic conditions (Liu et al., 2024a), which often leads to aggregation, flocculation and emulsion instability during storage (Yu et al., 2025).

Overall, protein-polysaccharide complexes improve the emulsion performance through steric hindrance, interfacial reinforcement, and enhanced environmental tolerance, exhibiting significantly better performance compared to single-protein stabilisers (Henao-Ardila et al., 2024; Hang et al., 2025; Kan et al., 2021; Tirgarian et al., 2022). Pectin, an anionic polysaccharide composed of α-1,4-linked galacturonic acid units, is a significant functional ingredient widely used in the food, pharmaceutical, and cosmetic industries (Kuang et al., 2024). Its functional behaviour is strongly influenced by the degree of esterification (DE). Studies indicate that high-DE pectin (74%) can synergistically enhance the solubility and emulsifying capacity of soy protein isolate by increasing hydrophilicity and steric hindrance (Ma et al., 2022). Similarly, medium-DE pectin (58%) has been shown to inhibit hemp seed protein aggregation and droplet coalescence by forming spatial barriers and reinforcing networks (Feng et al., 2021). However, other structural features such as molecular weight and galacturonic acid content also affect functionality (Morales-Contreras et al., 2024).

of the DE in governing the emulsification behaviour of pectin–PPI complexes has yet to be fully elucidated. As shown in Scheme 1, this study aimed to elucidate the molecular complexation mechanism between commercial PPI and pectins of varying DE. Three pectins were selected and divided into high (HDP), medium (MDP), and low (LDP) according to their DE value, aiming to determine how it governs the stability of PPI-based emulsions. The DE-dependent complexation mechanism was first systematically investigated by examining its relative contributions to hydrophobic, hydrogen bonding, and electrostatic interactions, along with the effects on protein conformation changes as revealed by spectroscopy. Subsequently, the molecular-level understanding of macroscopic functionality was elucidated by examining the physicochemical properties (e.g., solubility, droplet size, microstructure, rheology) and long-term stability of pectin-PPI-stabilised emulsions.

web.title: On the stability of acid-soluble pea protein-stabilized beverage emulsions against salt addition and heat treatment
web.description:
cheaper.8 However, similar to other plant proteins, pea proteins are intractable due to their poor aqueous solubility and sensitivity to pH, salt addition and temperature, which limit their applications.9 Therefore, finding a way to modulate and improve their functionality is highly sought after.

environments.19 Others have changed the pH of a globulin-rich pea protein isolate (extracted via isoelectric precipitation) to pH 3 before making an emulsion and proposed that a combination of particle-based Pickering and molecular proteins is responsible for the emulsifying property under an acidic environment.22,23 However, there is no knowledge of the emulsification ability and emulsion stability of albumin-rich acidic pea protein fractions under various environmental stresses. Therefore, this study aimed to mildly fractionate pea protein concentrate at an acidic pH 2.0 and utilize the acidic water-soluble pea protein (ASPP) fraction for stabilizing oil-in-water emulsions also in an acidic condition (pH 2.0) appropriate for beverage applications. The stability of these acidic emulsions in the presence of various levels of salt (NaCl) and heat treatment appropriate for beverage processing was also investigated. Moreover, the compositional and structural properties of the ASPP were also evaluated in relation to their functional properties and emulsion stabilization ability under various environmental stresses. The knowledge generated will improve our mechanistic understanding of the functionality of albumin-rich acidic pea proteins and may provide a promising way to manufacture stable acidic beverage emulsions using plant proteins.

Many studies have shown a lower emulsifying ability for pea protein at acidic pH than neutral and alkaline pH values.24,56 In another recent study, O/W emulsions were prepared with the soluble fraction of pea protein extracted at pH 7.0, which showed a D4,3 of 0.344 μm at pH 7.0, but upon changing the pH of the emulsion to pH 2.0, D4,3 increased to a much larger size (3.8 μm) due to extensive protein aggregation.19 The higher albumin content of ASPP extracted at low pH could be responsible for its improved emulsion formation ability under acidic pH.

web.title: Effect of high methoxyl pectin on pea protein in aqueous solution and at oil/water interface
web.description:
Particularly, protein-stabilized emulsions are sensitive to environmental conditions such as pH and ionic strength and will tend to flocculate at pH values close to the PI of the adsorbed proteins and when the ionic strength exceeds a certain level. Droplet flocculation is usually prevented in emulsions stabilized by adsorbed proteins due to the relatively strong electrostatic repulsion between the charged droplets at pH values far from the PI. For their part, and despite they are less surface active, polysaccharides, such as pectin, gum arabic and modified starch, produced emulsions that are often more resistant to changes in pH, ionic strength, and high temperatures than those stabilized by proteins (McClements, 2004). This was attributed to the fact that the interfacial polysaccharide membrane is more porous and thicker 0144-8617/$ -see front matter Ó 2009 Elsevier Ltd.

Particularly, pea proteins may be used to stabilize oil-in-water emulsions because of the surface properties of their constitutive protein units: the storage globulins 7S (vicilin) and 11S (legumin) (Guéguen, 1989). It has been shown recently that pea proteins are able to decrease the interfacial tension between the water and oil and help to stabilize emulsions by forming a rigid membrane at the oil-water interface (Ducel, Richard, Popineau, & Boury, 2004a;Ducel, Richard, Saulnier, Popineau, Boury, 2004b). However, environmental factors such as pH, ionic strength, or the presence of other ingredients will affect the stabilizing behavior of pea proteins in food emulsions (Guéguen, Chevalier, Barbot, & Schaeffer, 1988). Recently, Ducel, Saulnier, Richard, and Boury (2005) used the soft particle analysis to show that pea globulins have a spherical shape and high positive charge density at low pH. In these conditions, they have demonstrated that a relatively poorly charged polysaccharide having a rod-like structure is more convenient to allow a good overlapping of the charges of the two polymers than a strongly charged and spherical polysaccharide. Thus, high methoxyl pectin was selected in this work as a potential stabilizer of PPI-stabilized emulsions because it is a linear anionic polyelectrolyte (Thakur, Rakesh, & Handa, 1997) usually used as a thickening agent in food products. Moreover, it has been shown recently that pectin can strongly interact with interfacial adsorbed proteins at different physico-chemical conditions. Thus, it has been demonstrated that, at pH values below their PI, soy proteins (Lam, Shen, Paulsen, & Corredig, 2007) and whey proteins (Zaleska, Ring, & Tomasik, 2000) are able to form complexes with pectin chains. The presence of high methoxyl pectin in the aqueous phase during the formation of emulsions stabilized by caseins leads to some incorporation of polysaccharide into the interfacial stabilizing oil/water film at pH 5.5, but not at pH 7 (Dickinson et al., 1998). In the same way, by using diffusing wave spectroscopy, it has been shown that high methoxyl pectin is able to adsorb onto the sodium caseinate stabilized oil droplet under acidification conditions (Bonnet, Corredig, & Alexander, 2005). This adsorption was shown to allow, in the studied concentrated systems, to changes in oil droplet size and to emulsion stabilization by forming a network of oil droplets loosely connected by strands of pectin. Interfacial protein-polysaccharide complex formation (Dickinson, 2003), as well as properties of multilayer emulsions (Guzey & McClements, 2006a), were recently well reviewed. Particularly, more details about emulsions stabilized by proteins, hydrocolloids, and their combination can be found in a recent review (Dickinson, 2009). The purpose of the present work is to understand the origin of high methoxyl pectin-pea protein interactions in aqueous solutions and emulsions. Therefore, the behavior of pectin-PPI mixtures and their emulsion-stabilizing properties were evaluated in buffer solutions and in 5 wt.% oil-in-water emulsions, respectively. Changes caused by the addition of pectin to aqueous solutions and oil-in-water emulsions were studied in details at two pH values: below (pH 2.4) and above (pH 7) the isoelectric point of pea globulins ($4.3). However, pectin-PPI interaction diagrams were constructed for a larger pH range from 2.4 to 8. In order to provide a deeper insight into the consequences of pectin-pea protein interactions allowing to stabilization of oil-water interfaces at low pH values, drop tensiometer measurements are used to understand the effect of these interactions on the mechanical properties of the oil-water interface.

determination The lowest unadsorbed biopolymer concentration required to cause depletion flocculation is referred to as the critical flocculation concentration (CFC), which depends on the dimensions of the biopolymer molecules and the size of the emulsion droplets. We therefore examined the trend of pectin and maltodextrins having various DE to promote depletion flocculation in primary (5 wt.% oil, 0.25 wt.% PPI, 0.02 wt.% NaN 3 ) and secondary (5 wt.% oil, 0.25 wt.% PPI, 0.2 wt.% pectin, 0.02 wt.% NaN 3 ) emulsions.

A high turbid solutions containing solid precipitates were observed both (i) at low pectin concentrations (<0.05 wt.%) and low pH (2.4, 3 and 4) and (ii) at pH 3 and pH 4 at high pectin concentrations (P0.075 wt.%). The formation of these precipitates can be explained by three different mechanisms. (i) at pH 4 and low pectin concentrations, the overall net charge on the protein molecules is low, the precipitate can be attributed to the protein aggregation at pH values near the protein’s PI (3.5) (Thakur et al., 1997). We can therefore suppose, in this case, that the low charged protein molecules could form bridges between highly charged pectin ones at high pectin concentrations.

In fact, it has been shown that pea legumin exhibits a hexameric structure (11S type) which is maintained only in the pH range from 7 to 9. Decreasing the pH leads to a dissociation with a mixture of intermediary conformations at pH 3.4 and a complete dissociation leading to 3S components at pH 2.4 (Guéguen et al., 1988). This dissociation is able to modify the protein surface hydrophobicity (Guéguen, 1989) and probably the surface charge distribution, leading to make interactions with pectin possible even at pH values above the PI (turbid solutions obtained at pH 5 and 6) (Turgeon et al., 2007).

The high initial turbidity of about 0.75 cm À1 at pH 2.4, when pectin concentration was 0.0125 wt.%, denotes the presence of a large amount of dispersed high size pectin-PPI complexes as was confirmed by microscopy. This observed high size complex formation is in agreement with the previously evocated hypothesis of the formation of pectin bridges between protein molecules at low pH and low pectin concentrations. As can be derived from the drop of the turbidity value to reach a plateau of about 0.5 cm À1 when pectin concentration reaches 0.05 wt.% at pH 2.4, the particulate pectin-PPI complexes were gradually dissociated to give smaller complexes having a pectin concentration independent size.

To monitor how the net charge of formed complexes changes upon titration with pectin, the f-potential of the complexes was measured as a function of pectin concentration. At pH 2.4, the f-potential of the formed complexes (Fig. 3) changed from positive to negative as the pectin concentration was increased, indicating that the anionic polysaccharide molecules adsorbed to the cationic protein molecules through electrostatic attraction. The negative charge of the complexes reached a plateau value at a pectin concentration of approximately 0.0375 wt.%, which indicated that the protein molecules were ’’saturated“ with pectin chains around this concentration (Harnsilawat, Pongsawatmanit, & McClements, 2006). It is important to note that the pectin concentration of 0.0125 wt.% giving the largest volume complexes at pH 2.4 (Fig. 2) is the closest ratio to the electric equivalence point at this pH (Fig. 3) leading to precipitation of insoluble pectin-protein complexes. At pH 7 (Fig. 3), the f-potential of the mixture decreases from À15.6 mV (protein alone) to À18.6 mV at pectin concentration of 0.0875 wt.%, which is close the f-potential of pectin molecules alone at this pH.

It can be concluded from Figs. 1-3 that the increase of turbidity upon addition of pectin to protein together with a reduction of positive net charge indicates that protein molecules effectively bind pectin added to the solution at pH from 2.4 to 6 through mainly electrostatic interactions. Similar results have showed that formation of pea globulin-arabic gum complexes with a dense network are mainly due to electrostatic interactions but hydrogen bonds and hydrophobic interactions were shown to reinforce the packing of these complexes (Ducel, Pouliquen, Richard, & Boury, 2008). 3.2. Pectin-pea protein interactions in emulsions Oil-in-water emulsions were prepared containing 0.25 wt.% of PPI and different concentrations of pectin at pH ranging from 2.4 to 8 and a phase diagram of pectin concentration against pH was established as shown in Fig. 4. This phase diagram shows seven distinct regions: (1) at low pH and low pectin concentrations, negatively charged pectin molecules can interact with positively charged protein-stabilized oil droplets but there is no enough pectin to neutralize all protein positively charged groups. A single pectin molecule could adsorb to the surface of more than one emulsion droplet, thus acting as a polymeric link that promotes bridging flocculation (Guzey & McClements, 2006a); (2) above the EEP curve (curve a), the global electric charge of pectin-oil droplet complexes is negative but oil droplets are not completely saturated with pectin and bridging flocculation still occurs; (3) when pectin reached concentrations permitting to obtain monomodal particle size distribution (curve b), fine negatively charged pectin-protein complex coated oil droplets are obtained. Pectin concentration necessary to obtain stable multilayer emulsions decreased with increasing the pH mainly because of the decrease of the protein positive charge; (4) if pectin concentration exceeds certain levels (curve c), depletion flocculation caused by unadsorbed pectin molecules occurs. The amount of pectin able to induce depletion flocculation of pectin-protein complex stabilized emulsions was shown to slightly increase with increasing the pH (curve c) probably because of the increase of the adsorbed pectin negative charge when the pH increases. This could result in an increase in the repulsive forces between pectin coated oil droplets and consequently higher bulk pectin concentrations are needed to cause flocculation; (5) at pH values close to the protein PI ($4.3), it was not possible to obtain protein-stabilized emulsions; (6, 7) at pH values above the protein PI, the unadsorbed anionic polysaccharide induced depletion flocculation of the negatively charged proteincoated droplets. In this latter case, the pectin CFC increases with increasing the pH (curve d) probably because of the increase of protein negative charge when pH is increased. Moreover, at pH 6, flocculation occurs at relatively low pectin concentration because probably of an added bridging effect due to possible pectin-PPI interactions at this pH as it was suggested for aqueous mixtures of pectin and PPI in this range of pH (Fig. 1).

At pH 2.4, emulsion stability decreased rapidly (serum separation) for pectin concentration ranged between 0.01 and 0.05 wt.% and then increased again (Fig. 5). A slight destabilization was also observed at high polysaccharide concentrations (2.5 cm À1 ). The serum phase of pectin destabilized emulsions at pH 2.4 was clear compared to the turbid one of the destabilized emulsions at pH 7.

Indeed, at pH 2.4 and low pectin concentration, there was insufficient pectin present to completely saturate the droplet surfaces so bridging flocculation occurred. This type of bridging mechanism has been reported previously for protein-stabilized emulsions containing low concentration of ionic polysaccharides like carrageenan (Dickinson & Pawlowsky, 1997;Singh, Tamehana, Hemar, & Munro, 2003), dextran sulphate (Jourdain, Leser, Schmitt, Michel, & Dickinson, 2008) or pectin (Guzey, Kim, & McClements, 2004).
